key_insight: Composed Video Retrieval must reason about implicit after-effects (motion, state transitions, viewpoint, duration) implied by a textual edit; CoVR-R is a reasoning-first, zero-shot method that uses large multimodal models to infer those consequences and produce better retrieval queries.
problem_solved: Existing CoVR approaches assume the edit text fully specifies visual changes and miss implicit consequences, causing retrieval failures. This work addresses the gap by explicitly modeling and incorporating reasoning about after-effects so retrieved videos match both explicit edits and their implicit visual outcomes.
method: Use large multimodal models to perform zero-shot reasoning over a reference video + textual modification and predict implicit consequences (e.g., motion, state changes, viewpoint, duration).
Enrich or reformulate the retrieval query/representation with the inferred after-effects to create a more descriptive composed query.
Run zero-shot retrieval with off-the-shelf video-text encoders using the reasoning-augmented query, improving match quality without additional supervised fine-tuning.
impact: Makes composed video retrieval more accurate and generalizable by filling in unspoken visual consequences of edits, enabling practitioners to deploy stronger zero-shot systems and gain interpretable reasoning traces without heavy dataset-specific training.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: reference video + edit text -> LMM reasoning module -> enriched query -> retrieval results
Before/After example: thumbnail of reference video, the edit instruction, and the retrieved target video illustrating inferred changes (motion/viewpoint/duration)
Embedding/score plot: retrieval ranking comparison (baseline vs. CoVR-R) or t-SNE showing better clustering of intended targets
Icon set: motion arrow, clock (duration), camera (viewpoint), state-transition node to symbolize types of inferred after-effects
